p: Colgrove's charge is still debated. Some accounts suggest the order was given in confusion, that it was never meant to be a frontal assault across open ground. Whatever the intent, the result was exactly what Mudge had predicted.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Mudge and the Charge at Culp's Hill”, paragraph 13 of 14

p: His last words — 'It is murder but it is the order' — are among the most quoted of the battle.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Mudge and the Charge at Culp's Hill”, paragraph 14 of 14

p: General John Imboden had been ordered to prepare for the retreat. He was waiting near Lee's headquarters when the survivors of Pickett's Charge began coming back across the fields.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Lee Meets His Men”, paragraph 1 of 13

p: Lee rode out to meet them.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Lee Meets His Men”, paragraph 2 of 13

p: He rode slowly along the broken line of men, and Imboden watched from nearby. What he saw, he wrote later, he never forgot.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Lee Meets His Men”, paragraph 3 of 13

p: Lee rode among his men and said to them, over and over: 'All this has been my fault — it is I who have lost this fight, and you must help me out of it the best you can.' Some of the men reached up and touched his boots as he passed. Some wept.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Lee Meets His Men”, paragraph 4 of 13

p: When Pickett came to him, Lee said: 'Come, General Pickett. This has been my fight, and upon my shoulders rests the blame.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Lee Meets His Men”, paragraph 5 of 13

p: That night, Lee found Imboden waiting for him.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Lee Meets His Men”, paragraph 6 of 13

p: 'General,' Imboden said, 'this has been a hard day on you.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Lee Meets His Men”, paragraph 7 of 13

p: Lee said nothing at first. He sat on his horse in the darkness. Then he began to talk, and Imboden wrote down what he said as carefully as he could remember:

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Lee Meets His Men”, paragraph 8 of 13

p: 'I never saw troops behave more magnificently than Pickett's division of Virginians did today in that grand charge upon the enemy. And if they had been supported as they were to have been — but for some reason not yet fully explained — the charge would have been gloriously successful.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Lee Meets His Men”, paragraph 9 of 13

p: Then Lee fell silent again. He seemed to be speaking almost to himself.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Lee Meets His Men”, paragraph 10 of 13

p: 'Too bad. Too bad. Oh, too bad.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Lee Meets His Men”, paragraph 11 of 13

p: Imboden heard him say it over and over as they rode back toward headquarters.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Lee Meets His Men”, paragraph 12 of 13

p: Lee never said it quite so plainly again.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Lee Meets His Men”, paragraph 13 of 13
